## What is a Stochastic Process?

:::{.definition data-title="Stochastic Process"}

A **stochastic process** $X_t$ is a parameterized collection of
[[random-variables|random variables]] $(X_t)_{t\in T}$ defined on a
[[probability-spaces|probability space]]
$(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ and assuming values in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

:::

- The parameter space $T$ usually represents time, either as discrete
  increments $\{0,1,2,...,T\}$ or as a continuous interval $[0,\infty)$.
- Note that for each $t\in T$ fixed we have a random variable
  $\omega\rightarrow X_t(\omega)$ for $\omega\in\Omega$. On the other hand,
  fixing $\omega\in\Omega$ we can consider a **path** of $X_t$ as the function
  $t\rightarrow X_t(\omega)$ for $t\in T$.
- It is useful to think of $t$ as **time** and $\omega$ as a **realization** of
  the process.

## Types of Stochastic Process

Broadly speaking, stochastic processes can be classified into 4 groups:

1. **Discrete time and discrete state processes:**
    - Examples: [[markov-chains]], [[gwb-branching-processes|branching processes]],
      [[random-walks]].
2. **Discrete time and continuous state processes:**
    - Examples: [[arma-processes|ARMA models]], [[garch-models|GARCH models]].
3. **Continuous time and discrete state processes:**
    - Examples: [[poisson-process|Poisson processes]],
      [[birth-death-processes]].
4. **Continuous time and continuous state processes:**
    - Examples: [[brownian-motion]], [[ornstein-uhlenbeck-process]],
      [[geometric-brownian-motion]].

## Stochastic Process as a Random Function  

A stochastic process can be viewed as a single random element taking values
in a space of functions. The map $\omega\mapsto(t\mapsto X_t(\omega))$ sends each
outcome to a path in the space of functions $T\to\mathbb{R}^n$, and the
process is determined in law by its **finite-dimensional distributions**,
the joint laws of $(X_{t_1},\dots,X_{t_k})$ for all finite choices of times
$t_1,\dots,t_k\in T$. For continuous time, properties of paths such as
continuity are not determined by these alone; see
[[kolmogorovs-continuity-theorem]]. The information revealed up to time $t$ is
modelled by a filtration, see [[filtrations-and-adapted-processes]], and
random times that depend only on this information are
[[stopping-times]].
